title: Genuina principia doctrinae de statu aequilibrii et motu corporum tam perfecte flesibilium quam elasticorum

deep.reconstruction:
Context: E410 (Novi Commentarii 15 for 1770, printed 1771) begins with a plane thread or rod in equilibrium. Euler wants the internal force acting across a point M. On the previous page he imagines cutting off the lower part AM and asks what force applied at M keeps the upper part BM in its old state. He also notes that pinning BM at any point, even at the neighbouring point m, does not change that force.

§IV: With BM pinned at m, only the infinitesimal element Mm is free. Any force at M can only (i) pull Mm away from m or (ii) bend it about m. If the thread is perfectly flexible, it cannot resist bending, so no bending action is admissible at M. Otherwise Mm would at once rotate about m. Hence the internal force must act along Mm, that is, along the tangent mMT. In modern terms, the contact force in an ideal string is a pure tension along the tangent.

§V: If the thread is elastic and is curved at m, a tangential force alone cannot hold Mm in place. Curvature 'demands' a bending action. The curvature is judged from the next tangent mt, through the elementary angle Tmt, to which it is taken to be proportional (curvature = dφ/ds). So besides the tangential force there must be an oblique force whose moment sustains the curvature at m.

§VI (continued on the next page): this extra action is modelled as a force V normal to MT, applied at distance v along a rigid rod attached to the element. The moment Vv equals the elastic bending moment, which is fixed by the constitutive law (proportional to curvature). This gives the decomposition of the internal action into tension T, a normal (shear) force V and a bending moment Vv. Euler then transfers T, V and v differentially to m to obtain the equilibrium equations.
errors: No real error. The device of a normal force V at lever arm v on a fictitious rigid rod packs a shear force and a couple into one force. The finite moment Vv on an evanescent element only makes sense if v is finite (or V is large). Euler handles this correctly in the following sections, and Truesdell discusses it.
The argument that a perfectly flexible element cannot carry a normal force at M is heuristic: it treats Mm as rigid and pinned. The conclusion (tension is tangential) is correct.

ideas.what: Cut (section) principle: the internal force at a point is found by cutting the body and asking what force at the cut keeps the remainder in its state.
ideas.modern_name: Euler's cut principle / method of sections; contact force (precursor of the stress principle)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (E410 is the standard citation via Truesdell); generalised by Cauchy (1822)
ideas.where_published: E410 itself; discussed by Truesdell, Rational Mechanics of Flexible or Elastic Bodies 1638-1788 (Opera omnia II.11.2)

ideas.what: In a perfectly flexible thread the internal force is tangential.
ideas.usually_credited_to: Jakob Bernoulli / Johann Bernoulli / Euler (earlier catenary work)
ideas.where_published: Earlier Euler and Bernoulli string and catenary works; E410

ideas.what: In an elastic rod, curvature (measured by the angle between neighbouring tangents) requires a bending moment proportional to it, supplied together with a normal force.
ideas.modern_name: Bending moment and shear force in a planar rod (Euler–Bernoulli constitutive law M = EI·κ)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Jakob Bernoulli (moment–curvature law); Euler (E410, with shear force and moment as separate internal actions)
ideas.where_published: E65 Additamentum De curvis elasticis (1744); E410; Truesdell 1960

deep.surprise_reason: This is the well-known section of E410 that Truesdell singled out as the origin of the general principle of internal contact forces (tension, shear and moment in rods). It is fully documented in the literature.
